questions.q: If the plane $2x - y + 2z + 3 = 0$ has the distances $\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $\dfrac{2}{3}$ units from the planes $4x - 2y + 4z + \lambda = 0$ and $2x - y + 2z + \mu = 0$ , respectively, then the maximum value of $\lambda + \mu$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
The distance between the parallel planes $ax + by + cz + {d}_{1} = 0$ and $ax + by + cz + {d}_{2} = 0$ is $\dfrac{\left|{d}_{1} - {d}_{2}\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}} .$

Given, the distance between the planes $2x - y + 2z + 3 = 0$ and $4x - 2y + 4z + \lambda = 0, ⇒ 2x - y + 2z + \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = 0$ is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ units

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|\dfrac{\lambda}{2} - 3\right|}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|\dfrac{\lambda}{2} - 3\right|}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ \left|\dfrac{\lambda}{2} - 3\right| = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{\lambda}{2} - 3 = 1$ or $\dfrac{\lambda}{2} - 3 = - 1$

$⇒ \lambda = 8$ or $\lambda = 4 .$

Also, distance between the planes $2x - y + 2z + 3 = 0$ and $2x - y + 2z + \mu = 0$ is $\dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|µ - 3\right|}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|µ - 3\right|}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ \left|µ - 3\right| = 2$

$⇒ µ - 3 = 2$ or $µ - 3 = - 2$

$⇒ µ = 5$ or $⇒ µ = 1 .$

Hence, the maximum value of $\lambda + \mu = 8 + 5 = 13 .$

questions.q: A perpendicular is drawn from a point on the line $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1}$ to the plane $x + y + z = 3$ such that the foot of the perpendicular $Q$ also lies on the plane $x - y + z = 3$. Then the coordinates of $Q$ are
questions.solution:
The given line is $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1} = \lambda, ($let$)$

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \lambda, \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \lambda, \dfrac{z}{1} = \lambda$

$⇒ x = 2\lambda + 1, y = - \lambda - 1, z = \lambda .$

Hence, any point on the line is $\left(2\lambda + 1, - \lambda - 1, \lambda\right) .$

Thus, the point $P$ on the line is $\left(2\lambda + 1, - \lambda - 1, \lambda\right) .$

We know that the foot of perpendicular from a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right)$ on the plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ is $\dfrac{x - {x}_{1}}{a} = \dfrac{y - {y}_{1}}{b} = \dfrac{z - {z}_{1}}{c} = - \dfrac{\left(a{x}_{1} + b{y}_{1} + c{z}_{1}\right)}{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}} .$

Thus, the foot of perpendicular $Q$ from $P$ on the plane $x + y + z - 3 = 0$ is given by

$\dfrac{x - 2\lambda - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + \lambda + 1}{1} = \dfrac{z - \lambda}{1} = - \dfrac{\left(2\lambda - 3\right)}{3}$

$∵ Q$ lies on $x + y + z = 3 \text{ and } x - y + z = 3$

On adding the two equations, we get $y = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{\lambda + 1}{1} = \dfrac{- 2\lambda + 3}{3}$

$⇒ \lambda = 0$

Hence, we have $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{z}{1} = - \dfrac{\left(- 3\right)}{3}$

$⇒ x = 2, z = 1$

So, the coordinate of $Q$ are $\left(2, 0, 1\right) .$

Thus, the direction ratios of $AD$ are $=$

Using family of planes, equation to plane passing through the line of intersection of the given planes, is

If a plane is perpendicular to $xy$ plane, then it doesn't contain the term of $z .

Hence, $\lambda + 1 = 0 ⇒ \lambda = - 1 .

Thus,$ the plane isx + 2y + 11 = 0$

The length of perpendicular from a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right)$ to the plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ is $\dfrac{\left|a{x}_{1} + b{y}_{1} + c{z}_{1} + d\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}}$

questions.q: A plane passing though the points $( 0, - 1,0 )$ and $( 0, 0,1 )$ and making an angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with the plane $y – z + 5 = 0,$ also passes through the point
questions.solution:
The equation of a plane passing through a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right)$ and having direction ratios of the normal to the plane as is $a\left(x - {x}_{1}\right) + b\left(y - {y}_{1}\right) + c\left(z - {z}_{1}\right) = 0 .

Thus, the equation of the plane passing through \left(0, - 1, 0\right) is
$a$\left(x - 0\right)$ + b$\left(y + 1\right)$ + c$\left(z - 0\right)$ = 0$

$⇒ ax + by + cz + b = 0$

$∵$ It passes through \left(0, 0, 1\right)

$⇒ c = - b$

$∴$ Equation of plane is $ax + by - bz + b = 0 \ldots $\left(i\right)$

$∵$ It makes angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ with plane $y - z + 5 = 0$

The angle $\theta$ between the planes ${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y + {c}_{1}z + {d}_{1} = 0 and {a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y + {c}_{2}z + {d}_{2} = 0$ is defined as $cos\theta = \dfrac{\left|{a}_{1}{a}_{2} + {b}_{1}{b}_{2} + {c}_{1}{c}_{2}\right|}{\sqrt{{a}_{1}^{2} + {b}_{1}^{2} + {c}_{1}^{2}} \times \sqrt{{a}_{2}^{2} + {b}_{2}^{2} + {c}_{2}^{2}}}$

$⇒ cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\left|0 + b + b\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {b}^{2}} \times \sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\left|2b\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + 2{b}^{2}} \times \sqrt{2}}$

Squaring both sides, we get

$⇒ {a}^{2} + 2{b}^{2} = 4{b}^{2}$

$⇒ {a}^{2} = 2{b}^{2}$

$⇒ a = \pm \sqrt{2}b$

$∴$ Equation of plane is $\pm \sqrt{2}bx + by - bz + b = 0$

$⇒ \pm \sqrt{2}x + y - z + 1 = 0$

$∴$ Option $\left(\sqrt{2}, 1, 4\right)$ satisfies the given equation.

questions.q: If the line, $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{3} = \dfrac{z - 2}{4}$ meets the plane, $x + 2y + 3z = 15$ at a point $P,$ then the distance of $P$ from the origin is,
questions.solution:
Let $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{3} = \dfrac{z - 2}{4} = \lambda$

Let, coordinate of any point on line is $P = \left(2\lambda + 1, 3\lambda - 1, 4\lambda + 2\right)$

If $P$ is intersection point of plane & line then $P$ will lie on plane $x + 2y + 3z = 15$

$∴ \left(2\lambda + 1\right) + 2\left(3\lambda - 1\right) + 3\left(4\lambda + 2\right) = 15$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$∴ P = \left(2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 1, 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} - 1, 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 2\right) = \left(2, \dfrac{1}{2}, 4\right)$

The distance of a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right)$ from origin $O$ is $\sqrt{{\left({x}_{1}\right)}^{2} + {\left({y}_{1}\right)}^{2} + {\left({z}_{1}\right)}^{2}}$

$∴ OP = \sqrt{{2}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} + {4}^{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{81}{4}} = \dfrac{9}{2}$units.

questions.solution:
Planes passing through line of intersection of the planes $x + y + z = 1 and 2x + 3y + 4z = 5$ is
$\left(x + y + z - 1\right) + \lambda\left(2x + 3y + 4z - 5\right) = 0$
$⇒ ( 1 + 2\lambda ) x + ( 1 + 3\lambda ) y + ( 1 + 4\lambda ) z - ( 1 + 5\lambda ) = 0$

$1 ⋅ ( 1 + 2\lambda ) - 1 ⋅ ( 1 + 3\lambda ) + 1 ⋅ ( 1 + 4\lambda ) = 0 ⇒ \lambda = - \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.q: Let $S$ be the set of all real values of $\lambda$ such that a plane passing through the points $\left(- {\lambda}^{2}, 1, 1\right), \left(1, - {\lambda}^{2}, 1\right) and \left(1, 1, - {\lambda}^{2}\right) also passes through the point \left(- 1, - 1, 1\right). Then $S$ is equal to :$
questions.solution:
As we know that if four points $P, A, B, C$ are coplanar, the vectors $\overset{\to}{PA}, \overset{\to}{PB}, \overset{\to}{PC}$ must be coplanar.

$⇒ \overset{\to}{PA} . \left(\overset{\to}{PB} \times \overset{\to}{PC}\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}- {\lambda}_{}^{2} + 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & - {\lambda}^{2} + 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & - {\lambda}^{2} - 1\end{cases}\right| = 0$

$⇒ \left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left[\left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left(- {\lambda}^{2} - 1\right) - 0\right] - 2\left[2\left(- {\lambda}^{2} - 1\right) - 0\right] + 0\left[4 - 2\left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\right] = 0$

$⇒ \left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{4} - 1\right) + 4\left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{2} - 1\right) + 4\left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left\{\left(- {\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{2} - 1\right) + 4\right\} = 0$

$⇒ - \left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{4} - 2{\lambda}^{2} + 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ - \left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right)\left({\lambda}^{2} - 3\right)\left({\lambda}^{2} + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = \pm \sqrt{3}$

Also, we know that a vector perpendicular to two vectors lie along the cross product of the two vectors.

Hence, $\overset{\to}{n} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 3 & - 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{n} = - 7\overset{^}{i} - 7\overset{^}{j} + 7\overset{^}{k}$

Thus, the direction ratios of the normal to the plane are .

Hence, the equation of the plane having direction ratios the normal to the plane as and passing through the point$\left(4, - 1, 2\right)$ is

$- 7\left(x - 4\right) - 7\left(y + 1\right) + 7\left(z - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ - 7x - 7y + 7z = - 7$

$⇒ x + y - z = 1$

From the given options only the point $\left(1, 1, 1\right)$ satisfy the equation of the plane.

Hence, the plane passes through the point $\left(1, 1, 1\right) .$

questions.q: A plane bisects the line segment joining the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(-3,4,5)$ at right angles. Then this plane also passes through the point.
questions.solution:
Since the plane bisects the line joining the points $(1,2,3) and (-3,4,5)$ then the plane passes through the midpoint of the line which is :

$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{1-3}{2}, \frac{2+4}{2}, \frac{5+3}{2}\right) \equiv \left(\frac{-2}{2},\right.&\left.\frac{6}{2}, \frac{8}{2}\right)\\
& \equiv(-1,3,4).
\end{aligned}

As plane cuts$ the line segment at right angle, so the direction cosines of the normal of the plane are(-3-1,4-2,5-3)=(-4,2,2)So the $equation of the plane is :

-4 x+2 y+2 z=\lambda

As plane passes through$(-1,3,4)$so

-4(-1)+2(3)+2(4)=\lambda \Rightarrow \lambda=18

Therefore, equation$ of plane is :

-4 x+2 y+2 z=18

Now, only(-3,2,1)$ satisfies the given plane as $-4(-3)+2(2)+2(1)=18

& \equiv(-1,3,4) .

$

questions.solution:
Direction ratio's of the plane perpendicular to two given lines is, $\overset{\to}{n} = \overset{\to}{n}1 \times \overset{\to}{n}2$

$= \overset{^}{i}\left(49 - 40\right) - \overset{^}{j}\left(42 - 24\right) + \overset{^}{k}\left(30 - 21\right)$

$= 9\overset{^}{i} - 18\overset{^}{j} + 9\overset{^}{k}$

Hence, $dr ' s = \left(9, - 18, 9\right)$

Now, plane passes through $\left(- 1, 1, 3\right)$ (A point on the first line),

Hence, the equation of plane containing lines is

$1\left(x + 1\right) - 2\left(y - 1\right) + \left(z - 3\right) = 0$

$⇒ x - 2y + z = 0$

$∴$ Foot of perpendicular of point $\left(1, - 2, 1\right)$ is

$\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 2}{- 2} = \dfrac{z - 1}{1} = - \dfrac{\left[1 + 4 + 1\right]}{6} = - 1$

$x - 1 = - 1, y + 2 = 2, z - 1 = - 1$

$x = 0, y = 0, z = 0$

questions.solution:
Any line parallel to $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{4} = \dfrac{z}{5}$ and passing through $P ( 1, - 2, 3 )$ is

$\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 2}{4} = \dfrac{z - 3}{5} = \lambda$ (say)

Any point on above line can be written as $( \lambda + 1, 4\lambda - 2, 5\lambda + 3 ) .$

$∴$ Coordinates of $R$ are $( \lambda + 1, 4\lambda - 2, 5\lambda + 3 ) .$

Since, point $R$ lies on the above plane. $∴ 2 ( \lambda + 1 ) + 3 ( 4\lambda - 2 ) - 4 ( 5\lambda + 3 ) + 22 = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = 1$

So, point $R$ is $( 2, 2, 8 )$

Now, $PR = \sqrt{( 2 - 1{)}^{2} + ( 2 + 2{)}^{2} + ( 8 - 3{)}^{2}} = \sqrt{42}$

$∴ PQ = 2PR = 2\sqrt{42}$

Since, point $R$ lies on the above plane.

So, point $R$ is $( 2, 2, 8 )$

questions.q: $ABC$ is a triangle in a plane with vertices A $\left(2, 3, 5\right), B \left(- 1, 3, 2\right) and C \left(\lambda, 5, \mu\right) . If the median through A$ is equally inclined to the coordinate axes, then the value of $\left({\lambda}^{3} + {\mu}^{3} + 5\right)$ is
questions.solution:
Let coordinate of mid-point of $BC$ is point $D$, then

$D ≡ \left(\dfrac{\lambda - 1}{2}, 4, \dfrac{\mu + 2}{2}\right)$

And, $A ≡ \left(2, 3, 5\right)$

Therefore, direction ratios of $AD$ are

$\left<\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 1}{2} - 2\right), \left(4 - 3\right), \left(\dfrac{\mu + 2}{2} - 5\right)\right>$

$\left<\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}, 1, \dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right>$

Hence, direction cosines of $AD$ are

$\left<\dfrac{\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}}, \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}}\right>$

Since, median $AD$ is making equal angles with coordinate axes, therefore

$\dfrac{\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}}{\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2}\right)}^{2} + 1 + {\left(\dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}\right)}^{2}}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\lambda - 5}{2} = 1 = \dfrac{\mu - 8}{2}$

$⇒$\lambda = 7and\mu = 10$

$∴ {\lambda}^{3} + {\mu}^{3} + 5 = 1348$

questions.q: Let $ABC$ be a triangle whose circumcentre is at $P$. If the position vectors $A, B, C$ and $P$ are $\overset{\to}{a}, \overset{\to}{b}, \overset{\to}{c}$ and $\dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c}}{4}$ respectively, then the position vector of the orthocentre of this triangle, is :
questions.solution:
$O$ is orthocentre and $G$ is centroid and $C$ is circumcentre. $G$ divides $OC$ in $2: 1$ ratio.
Position vector of centriod $\overset{\to}{G} = \dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c}}{3}$
Position vector of circum center $\overset{\to}{C} = \dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c}}{4}$
Apply Section Formula,
$\overset{\to}{G} = \dfrac{2\overset{\to}{C} + \overset{\to}{R}}{3}$

$3\overset{\to}{G} = 2\overset{\to}{C} + \overset{\to}{R}$

$\overset{\to}{R} = 3\overset{\to}{G} - 2\overset{\to}{C} = ( \overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c} ) - 2\left(\dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c}}{4}\right)$

$=\dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c}}{2}$

questions.q: The shortest distance between the lines $\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x + 2}{- 1} = \dfrac{y - 4}{8} = \dfrac{z - 5}{4},$ lies in the interval:
questions.solution:
Let the direction vectors of the two lines be given by-${a}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{1}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{1}\overset{^}{k} = 2\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$ and ${a}_{2}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{k} = - \overset{^}{i} + 8\overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}$

The shortest distance between the two lines is given by-

$\dfrac{\left(\left({x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left({y}_{2} - {y}_{1}\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left({z}_{2} - {z}_{1}\right)\overset{^}{k}\right) . \left[\left({a}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{1}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{1}\overset{^}{k}\right) \times \left({a}_{2}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)\right]}{\left|\left({a}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{1}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{1}\overset{^}{k}\right) \times \left({a}_{2}\overset{^}{i} + {b}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{k}\right)\right|}$

$= \left|\dfrac{\left|\begin{cases}{x}_{2} - {x}_{1} & {y}_{2} - {y}_{1} & {z}_{2} - {z}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2}\end{cases}\right|}{\left|\begin{cases}i & j & k \\ {a}_{1} & {b}_{1} & {c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{2}\end{cases}\right|}\right|$

$= \left|\dfrac{\left|\begin{cases}- 2 & 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ - 1 & 8 & 4\end{cases}\right|}{\left|\begin{cases}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ - 1 & 8 & 4\end{cases}\right|}\right| = \dfrac{54}{\sqrt{{9}^{2} + {18}^{2}}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}}$

Now $\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{9}} < \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}} < \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{4}} ⇒ 2 < \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{5}} < 3$

questions.q: The distance of the point $\left(1, - 2, 4\right)$ from the plane passing through the point $\left(1, 2, 2\right)$ and perpendicular to the planes $x - y + 2z = 3 and 2x - 2y + z + 12 = 0,$ is :
questions.solution:
Let equation of plane be

$a\left(x - 1\right) + b\left(y - 2\right) + c\left(z - 2\right) = 0$ .......$\left(i\right)$

Since $( i )$ is perpendicular to the given planes, then

Dot product of the normal vectors of the perpendicular planes is $0$.

$a - b + 2c = 0$

$2a - 2b + c = 0$

Solving above equations $c = 0 and a = b$ equation of plane $\left(i\right)$ becomes $x + y - 3 = 0$

Distance from $\left(1, - 2, 4\right)$ will be

$D = \dfrac{\left|1 - 2 - 3\right|}{\sqrt{1 + 1}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2}$

questions.solution:
We have,

Change it into symmetrical form

Put $z = 1,$ then

$x + y - 1 = 0$

$2x + 3y = 0$

On solving, we get

$x = 3, y = - 2, z = 1$

$\left(3, - 2, 1\right)$

Direction ratio of the line is

$= \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 4\end{cases}\right| = - 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{k}$

Hence, equation of line in symmetrical form is

$\dfrac{x - 3}{- 2} = \dfrac{y + 2}{0} = \dfrac{z - 1}{1}$

Equation of $z$ axis is, $\dfrac{x}{0} = \dfrac{y}{0} = \dfrac{z}{1}$

Shortest Distance $= \dfrac{\left|\begin{cases}3 & - 2 & 1 \\ - 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right|}{\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ - 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right|}$

$= \left|\dfrac{- 4}{2\overset{^}{j}}\right| = 2$

questions.q: If the shortest distance between the line $\dfrac{x - 1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1}, \left(\alpha \ne - 1\right)$, and $x + y + z + 1 = 0 = 2x - y + z + 3$ is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$,then value of $\alpha$ is :
questions.solution:
Let us change the line into symmetric form.

$x + y + z + 1 = 0 = 2x - y + z + 3$

Put $z = 1$ , so we get $x + y + 2 = 0$ and $2x - y + 4 = 0$

We will get $x = - 2$, $y = 0$

$∴$ The point $\left(- 2, 0, 1\right)$ lies on the line and perpendicular vector will come from $\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$

So the equation of line would be $\dfrac{x + 2}{2} = \dfrac{y}{1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{- 3}$
And the other line $\dfrac{x - 1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1}$
Shortest distance would be $D = \dfrac{\left|\left(\overset{\to}{{a}_{2}} - \overset{\to}{{a}_{1}}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{\to}{{b}_{1}} \times \overset{\to}{{b}_{2}}\right)\right|}{\left|\left(\overset{\to}{{b}_{1}} \times \overset{\to}{{b}_{2}}\right)\right|}$

When $\overset{\to}{{a}_{1}} = \left(- 2\overset{^}{i} + 0\overset{^}{j} + 1\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{{a}_{2}} = \left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 0\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{{b}_{1}} = 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{{b}_{2}} = \alpha\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

$= \dfrac{\left|3\left(1 - 3\right) + 1\left(2 + 3\alpha\right) + 1\left(2 + \alpha\right)\right|}{\left|- 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j}\left(2 + 3\alpha\right) + \overset{^}{k}\left(- 2 - \alpha\right)\right|}$

questions.q: The equation of the plane containing the line of intersection of $2x - 5y + z = 3; x + y + 4z = 5,$ and parallel to the plane, $x + 3y + 6z = 1,$ is
questions.solution:
Any plane containing the line of intersection of $2x - 5y + z = 3, x + y + 4z = 5$ will be of the form

$\left(2 x - 5 y + z - 3\right) + \lambda \left(x + y + 4 z - 5\right) = 0$

$\left(2 + \lambda\right) x - \left(5 - \lambda\right) y + \left(1 + 4 \lambda\right) z - \left(3 + 5 \lambda\right) = 0$

It is parallel to plane $x + 3 y + 6 z = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{2 + \lambda}{1} = \dfrac{\lambda - 5}{3} = \dfrac{1 + 4\lambda}{6} \ne \dfrac{\left(3 + 5\lambda\right)}{1}$

$\dfrac{2 + \lambda}{1} = \dfrac{\lambda - 5}{3} ⇒ 6 + 3 \lambda = \lambda - 5$

$2 \lambda = - 1 1$

$\lambda = \dfrac{- 1 1}{2}$

$∴$ Required plane is

$\left(2x - 5y + z - 3\right) + \dfrac{\left(- 11\right)}{2}\left(x + y + 4z - 5\right) = 0$

$2 \left(2 x - 5 y + z - 3\right) - 1 1 \left(x + y + 4 z - 5\right) = 0$

$4 x - 1 0 y + 2 z - 6 - 1 1 x - 1 1 y - 4 4 z + 5 5 = 0$

$- 7 x - 2 1 y - 4 2 z + 4 9 = 0$

$⇒ x + 3 y + 6 z - 7 = 0$

questions.q: If the angle between the line $2\left(x ⁡ + 1\right) = y ⁡ = z ⁡ + 4$ and the plane $2x ⁡ - y ⁡ + \sqrt{\lambda}z ⁡ + 4 = 0$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, then the value of $\lambda$ is
questions.solution:
Given line is $L: \dfrac{x + 1}{1} = \dfrac{y}{2} = \dfrac{z + 4}{2}$ and plane is $P:2x - y + \sqrt{\lambda} z + 4 = 0 .$

The angle between a line $\dfrac{x - {x}_{1}}{l} = \dfrac{y - {y}_{1}}{m} = \dfrac{z - {z}_{1}}{n}$ and a plane $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ is

$sin\theta = \dfrac{\left|al + bm + cn\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}\sqrt{{l}^{2} + {m}^{2} + {n}^{2}}}$


$sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\left|\left(2 \times 1\right) + \left(- 1 \times 2\right) + 2\sqrt{\lambda}\right|}{\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {2}^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2} + {1}^{2} + \lambda}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\left|2 - 2 + 2\sqrt{\lambda}\right|}{\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4}\sqrt{4 + 1 + \lambda}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\left|2\sqrt{\lambda}\right|}{3\sqrt{5 + \lambda}}$

$⇒ 4\sqrt{\lambda} = 3\sqrt{5 + \lambda}$

Squaring both sides, we get

$⇒ 16\lambda = 9\left(5 + \lambda\right)$

$⇒ 16\lambda = 45 + 9\lambda$

$⇒ 7\lambda = 45$

$⇒ \lambda = \dfrac{45}{7} .$

questions.q: Equation of the line of the shortest distance between the lines $\dfrac{x ⁡}{1} = \dfrac{y ⁡}{- 1} = \dfrac{z ⁡}{1}$ and $\dfrac{x ⁡ - 1}{0} = \dfrac{y ⁡ + 1}{- 2} = \dfrac{z ⁡}{1}$ is
questions.solution:
The equation of a line of the shortest distance between the given lines will be along the perpendicular to both the lines.

A line perpendicular to ${L}_{1}: \dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1}$ and ${L}_{2}: \dfrac{x - 1}{0} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 2} = \dfrac{z}{1}$ is,

$\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & - 1 & 1 \\ 0 & - 2 & 1\end{cases}\right| = \overset{^}{i}\left(- 1 + 2\right)$ - \overset{^}{j}$\left(1 - 0\right)$ + \overset{^}{k}$\left(- 2 + 0\right)$

$= \overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$

Let, $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{1} =$\alpha$

$⇒ x = \alpha, y = - \alpha, z = \alpha$

Thus, a point on the line ${L}_{1}$ is $P ( \alpha, - \alpha, \alpha )$

Similarly, let \dfrac{x - 1}{0} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 2} = \dfrac{z}{1} =$\lambda$

$⇒ x = 1, y = - 2\lambda - 1, z = \lambda$

Thus, a point on the line ${L}_{2}$ is $Q ( 1, - 1 - 2\lambda, \lambda )$

Now, a vector joining the points $P $\text{$ and } Q$ is $( \alpha - 1 ) \overset{^}{i} + ( 2\lambda - \alpha + 1 ) \overset{^}{j} + ( \alpha - \lambda ) \overset{^}{k}$

Let, the vector joining the points $P $\text{$ and } Q$ is along perpendicular to the two lines.

Hence, $( \alpha - 1 ) \overset{^}{i} + ( 2\lambda - \alpha + 1 ) \overset{^}{j} + ( \alpha - \lambda ) \overset{^}{k}$ and $\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$ are

proportional and hence on comparing, \dfrac{\alpha - 1}{1} = \dfrac{\alpha - 2\lambda - 1}{1} = \dfrac{\lambda - \alpha}{2}$

$⇒ \alpha - 1 = \alpha - 2\lambda - 1$

$⇒ \lambda = 0$

Hence, point $Q$ is $\left(1, - 1, 0\right)$

The equation of a line passing through a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}, {z}_{1}\right)$ and parallel to a vector $a\overset{^}{i} + b\overset{^}{j} + c\overset{^}{k}$ is $\dfrac{x - {x}_{1}}{a} = \dfrac{y - {y}_{1}}{b} = \dfrac{z - {z}_{1}}{c}$

So, the equation of required line is $\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z}{- 2} .

$

questions.solution:
Given two planes:
 
x-a y-b=0 $\text{$ and } c y-z+d=0
 
Let, $l, m, n$ be the direction ratio of the required line. Since the required line is perpendicular to normal of both the plane, therefore $l-a m=0$ and $c m-n=0 \Rightarrow l-a m+0 . n=0$ and $0 . l+c m-n=0 $

Hence, d.R of the required line are $a, 1$, $c$.
Hence, options (c) and (d) are rejected. Now, the point $(a+b, 1, c+d)$ satisfy the equation of the two given planes.
$\therefore$ Option (b) is correct.

questions.solution:
Line

${L}_{2}: \dfrac{x - 3}{1} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2} = \dfrac{z - 2}{3} = \mu$

$\begin{cases}⇒ x = 3\lambda + 1 & \text{and} & x = \mu + 3 \\ y = \lambda + 2 & & y = 2\mu + 1 \\ z = 2\lambda + 3 & & z = 3\mu + 2\end{cases}$

questions.q: The angle between the lines whose direction cosines satisfy the equations $l ⁡ + m + n = 0$ and $l{⁡}^{2} = {m}^{2} + {n}^{2}$ is
questions.solution:
$l ⁡+ m + n =0$

$m + n =- l ⁡$

$∴ {\left(m + n\right)}^{2} = l{⁡}^{2}$

$∴ l{⁡}^{2} = {m}^{2} + {n}^{2} + 2mn$

But, ${m}^{2} + {n}^{2} = l{⁡}^{2}$

$∴ 2 mn =0$

$∴ m = 0 or n = 0$

$∴ l ⁡ = - n or l ⁡ = - m$

$∵ l{⁡}^{2} + {m}^{2} + {n}^{2} = 1$

$∴$ The two direction cosines are $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, \dfrac{- 1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) and \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{- 1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{,}0\right)$

$\theta$ is the angle between them.

$∴ \text\cos\theta = {l}_{1}{l}_{2} + {m}_{1}{m}_{2} + {n}_{1}{n}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 + 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴ \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Note : Taking $l ⁡ = \dfrac{- 1}{\sqrt{2}}$, will also given the same solution, but the supplementary angle. Both are correct, we choose the one present in the options.

questions.q: The equation of a plane through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2 y=3, y-2 \mathrm{z}+1=0$, and perpendicular to the first plane is :
questions.solution:
Equation of a plane through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2 y=3, y-2 z+1=0$ is $(x+2 y-3)+\lambda(y-2 z+1)=0$
\Rightarrow x+(2+\lambda) y-2 \lambda(z)-3+\lambda=0

Now, plane (i) is $\perp$ to $x+2 y=3\therefore \quad$ Their dot product is zero
i.e. $1+2(2+\lambda)=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-\frac{5}{2}$
Thus, required plane is

$\begin{aligned}$& x+$\left(2-\frac{5}{2}$\right)$y-2 $\times $\frac{-5}{2}($z)-3-$\frac{5}{2}=0 \\
\Rightarrow & x-\frac{y}{2}$+$5 z-\frac{11}{2}$=$0 \\
\Rightarrow & 2 x-y+10 z-11=0
\end{aligned}
$

questions.solution:
Point is $(-1,2,6)$
Line passes through the point $(2,3,-4)$ parallel to vector whose direction ratios is $6,3,-4$.
Equation is $\frac{x-2}{6}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+4}{-4}=\lambda$
Any point on this line is given by $x=6$\lambda+2, y=3 \lambda+3, z=-4 \lambda-4$

So, $6(x+1)+3(y-2)-4(z-6)=0$\Rightarrow 6 x+3 y-4 z+24=0$
Now, $6(6 \lambda+2)+3(3 \lambda+3)+4(4 \lambda+4)$+24=0$\Rightarrow 61 \lambda+61=0 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1$
So, $x=-4, y=0, z=0$
Now, distance between $(-1,2,6)$ and $(-4,0,0)$ is
$\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7$

questions.q: If the three planes $x=5,2 x-5 a y+3 z-2=0$ and $3 b x+y-3 z=0$ contain a common line, then $(a, b)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let the direction ratios of the common line be $\ell, m$ and n.

$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore \ell $\times$1+$\mathrm{m} \times$0+$\mathrm{n} \times$0=0 \Rightarrow \ell=0 \\
& 2 \ell-5 m a+3 n=0 \Rightarrow 5 m a-3 n=0 \\
& 3 \ell b+m-3 n=0 \Rightarrow m-3 n=0
\end{aligned}

Subtracting (3)$ from (1), we getm(5 a-1)=0$
Now, value of $m$ can not be zero because if $m=0$ then $n=0\Rightarrow \ell=m=n=0$ which is not possible.
Hence, $5 a-1=0 \Rightarrow a=\frac{1}{5}$

questions.q: A unit vector which is perpendicular to the vector $2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and is coplanar with the vectors $\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $2 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}$ be the required unit vector.
Since $\hat{a}$ is perpendicular to $(2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k})$.

\therefore \quad 2 x-y+2 z=0

Since vector $x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}$ is coplanar with the vector $\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} and 2 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$.

$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad$x \hat{i} & +y \hat{j}+z \hat{k} \\
& =p(\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})+q(2 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}),
\end{aligned}

where $p and q$ are some scalars.

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k} \\
& =(p+2 q) \hat{i}+(p+2 q) \hat{j}-(p+q) \hat{k} \\
& \Rightarrow x=p+2 q, y=p+2 q, z=-p-q
\end{aligned}

Now$ from equation (i),\begin{aligned}$& 2 p+4 q-p-2 q-2 p-2 q=0 \\
\Rightarrow & -p=0 \Rightarrow p=0 \\
\therefore & x=2 q, y=2 q, z=-q
\end{aligned}

Since vector $x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}$ is a unit vector, therefore

$\begin{aligned}$& |x \hat{i}+y \hat{j}+z \hat{k}|=1 \\
\Rightarrow & $\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}=$1 \\
\Rightarrow & x²+y²+z²=1 \\
\Rightarrow & 4 q²+4 q²+q²=1
\end{aligned}

\Rightarrow 9 q²=1 \Rightarrow q=$\pm \frac{1}{3}$When $q=\frac{1}{3}$, then $x=\frac{2}{3}, y=\frac{2}{3}$,

z=-$\frac{1}{3}$When $q=-\frac{1}{3}$, then $x=-\frac{2}{3}, y=-\frac{2}{3}$,

z=$\frac{1}{3}$Here required unit vector is $\frac{2}{3} \hat{i}+\frac{2}{3} \hat{j}-\frac{1}{3} \hat{k}$ or $-\frac{2}{3} \hat{i}-\frac{2}{3} \hat{j}+\frac{1}{3} \hat{k}$.

questions.q: A line with direction cosines proportional to $2,1,2$ meets each of the lines $x=y+a=z$ and $x+a=2 y=2 z$. The co-ordinates of each of the point of intersection are given by
questions.solution:
Any point on the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+a}{1}=\frac{z}{1}=t_1 \quad$ (say) is $\left(t_1, t_1-a, t_1\right)$ and any point on the line $\frac{x+a}{2}=\frac{y}{1}=\frac{z}{1}=t_2 \quad($ say $)$ is $\left(2 t_2-a, t_2, t_2\right)$.
Now direction cosine of the lines intersecting the above lines is proportional to $\left(2 t_2-a-t_1, t_2-t_1+a, t_2-t_1\right)$.
Hence $2 \mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{a}-\mathrm{t}_1=2 \mathrm{k}, \mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{k}$ and $\mathrm{t}_2-\mathrm{t}_1=2 \mathrm{k}$
On solving these, we get $t_1=3 a, t_2=a$.
Hence points are $(3 a, 2 a, 3 a) and (a, a, a)$
